overview: This four-page U.S. Department of State “List of Papers” indexes correspondence and memoranda concerning Japanese news-gathering agencies and newspaper correspondents in the United States, chiefly during 1941–1942. The entries trace visa requests, reciprocal treatment of American and Japanese journalists, wartime detention and transfer to Hot Springs and White Sulphur Springs, repatriation aboard the Gripsholm, and efforts to recover automobiles, papers, and other personal property. Swiss and Spanish protecting-power representatives figure prominently, while several cross-references point to related State Department files on alien detention, exchange arrangements, and press privileges.

subfiles.title: Department of State list of papers on Japanese news-gathering agencies in the United States
subfiles.about: A four-page index summarizes papers on Japanese correspondents, reciprocal press treatment, wartime detention and repatriation, and disputes over journalists' property.
subfiles.summary: The list begins with Toichiro Takamatsu's efforts to obtain permission to remain temporarily in the United States and with diplomatic exchanges concerning reciprocal treatment of American and Japanese correspondents. Later entries concern the detention or transfer of Isamu Suzuki, Yoshiyuki Akiyama, Kyōzo Mori, Toshio Tomomatsu, Tokumaru Nishijima, and other Japanese press representatives to Hot Springs or White Sulphur Springs and their possible repatriation. Additional entries document Mori's attempts to recover an automobile and personal effects, reports on materials seized from the Dōmei Agency, cargo from the Sanyo Maru, and the accreditation of Swiss correspondent Georges-Henri Martin. The date in the heading appears with the DS-46 form, while the indexed papers themselves chiefly date from 1941 and 1942.

interest: The index is valuable as a compact roadmap to the wartime administration of enemy-country journalists, showing how press status intersected with immigration law, detention, diplomatic reciprocity, censorship, and civilian exchange. It also reveals the practical role of the Swiss and Spanish protecting powers in negotiating treatment and property claims after diplomatic relations had broken down. Its cross-references are especially useful for tracing dispersed records in related decimal-file series, while the entries concerning individual correspondents help reconstruct the personnel and overseas networks of major Japanese newspapers and agencies.
